sliceGuide: This snapshot is ~50k tokens. For targeted analysis fetch a slice: governance (CA/Browser Forum oversight, compliance, BR readiness, audit letter quality), distrust (16 distrust events 2011-2024 + incidents), market (CA market share, trust surface), risk (geographic, government, jurisdiction, full 317-root crypto data). Each slice is self-contained with generatedAt and snapshotUrl.

dataSources.crtSh: Certificate Transparency logs via crt.sh — unexpired and all-time precertificate counts per CA owner. Updated daily.
dataSources.ccadb: Common CA Database (AllCertificateRecordsCSVFormatv4) — root/intermediate metadata, trust store inclusion, CA owner details. Updated daily.
dataSources.bugzilla: Mozilla Bugzilla CA Certificate Compliance — incident reports, root program comments, CA responses. 2014-present. Updated daily.
dataSources.statcounter: StatCounter global browser market share — mapped to root programs for web coverage estimates. Updated daily.
dataSources.cabforum: CA/Browser Forum ballot records — proposers, endorsers, vote results across Server Certificate, Code Signing, S/MIME, and Network Security working groups.
dataSources.keylength: keylength.com — cryptographic key size recommendations from NIST, ECRYPT-CSA, BSI, ANSSI, and NSA CNSA.
dataSources.cabforumMembers: CA/B Forum membership roster — CA members, browser members, interested parties. Used for ecosystem participation baseline.
dataSources.chromeRootStore: Chrome Root Store git commit history — root additions and removals with timestamps.
dataSources.tabIntros: Analyst summaries generated daily by Claude Sonnet from the prior day's data digest. Each intro states the key finding for that tab with specific numbers and connects related tabs.
dataSources.regulatorySurface: Normative obligation counts across all CA compliance documents — CA/Browser Forum BRs (PDF archive 2012-2021 + GitHub tags 2021-present), root program policies, IETF RFCs (operative versions), NIS2 Directive (EUR-Lex), NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 (OSCAL). Four convention-aware parsers: RFC2119_INLINE, SHALL_LETTERED_LIST, EU_LEGAL, NIST_OSCAL. Ballot timeline from document revision history tables.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: Mandatory cooperation for all organizations (NIL Art. 7/14); full SCA access to systems and keys in critical information infrastructure (Cryptography Law Art. 31).

laws.name: National Intelligence Law (2017)
laws.excerpt: All organizations and citizens shall support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts in accordance with law.

laws.name: Cryptography Law (2019)
laws.excerpt: SCA and local agencies have complete access to the cryptography system and to the data protected by that system.

laws.name: Cybersecurity Law (2016)
laws.excerpt: Network operators shall provide technical support and assistance to public security organs and national security organs.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: FSB direct access via SORM; Yarovaya Law requires encryption key disclosure without court order.

laws.name: Yarovaya Law (2016)
laws.excerpt: Any online service that uses encrypted data is required to permit the FSB to access encrypted communications, including providing any encryption keys.

laws.name: SORM Regulations (1995+)
laws.excerpt: FSB has access to electronic messages and the keys to decrypt these without judicial authorization.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: RIPA s.49 compels key disclosure with up to 5yr penalty; IPA 2016 Technical Capability Notices; tipping-off ban prevents disclosure to auditors.

laws.name: RIPA 2000, Part III
laws.excerpt: A disclosure requirement is necessary if it is necessary (a) in the interests of national security; (b) for preventing or detecting crime; (c) in the interests of the economic well-being of the UK.

laws.name: Investigatory Powers Act 2016
laws.excerpt: Government can serve Technical Capability Notices requiring operators to remove electronic protection on communications on an ongoing basis.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: TOLA Act TANs/TCNs compel decryption assistance from broad DCP class; 5yr gag order penalty; 10yr for warrant non-compliance.

laws.name: Assistance and Access Act 2018 (TOLA)
laws.excerpt: DCPs include software developers, device manufacturers, and anyone who provides services that facilitate a carriage or electronic service.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: IT Act s.69 executive orders to intermediaries; no judicial oversight; 7yr penalty for noncompliance.

laws.name: Information Technology Act 2000 (amended 2008)
laws.excerpt: The subscriber or intermediary or any person in-charge of the computer resource shall assist the agency to intercept, monitor, or decrypt the information. Failure: imprisonment up to seven years.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: Judicial oversight required; CALEA limits carrier decryption duty; All Writs Act and NSLs (with gag) possible. Lavabit precedent for SSL keys.

laws.name: CALEA (1994)
laws.excerpt: A carrier shall not be responsible for decrypting any communication encrypted by a subscriber or customer, unless the encryption was provided by the carrier.

laws.name: NSLs / All Writs Act
laws.excerpt: Lavabit shut down rather than surrender its master private keys due to the government wanting to spy on Edward Snowden's emails.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: Judicial orders only; 3yr / €270K penalty for refusal.

laws.name: Code of Criminal Procedure
laws.excerpt: A judge may designate a technical expert to obtain plaintext from encrypted data seized during an investigation.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: TICSA requires interception capability; Search and Surveillance Act s.130 compels key access under warrant.

laws.name: TICSA (2013)
laws.excerpt: Network operators must decrypt communications if they have provided the encryption or hold the decryption key.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: RICA s.21 requires provider decryption assistance if key held. Key safeguards struck down by Constitutional Court in 2021; amendments pending.

laws.name: RICA 2002
laws.excerpt: Encrypted communications must be provided in decrypted form if the provider holds the decryption key.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: BTK orders for hosting/access providers; electronic communications law requires interception capability.

laws.name: Law No. 5651 (2007, amended)
laws.excerpt: Hosting and access providers must comply with government orders including providing access to encrypted data.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: E-Commerce Law Art. 43 prohibits encrypting evidence; untested but broadly worded.

laws.name: Law on Electronic Commerce (2019)
laws.excerpt: Prohibits any encryption of evidence in the form of data that could lead to an indictment, or any evidence in an electronic system that relates to an offense.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: Third-party (non-suspect) assistance only; judicial order required. GlobalSign incorporated here.

laws.name: Code of Criminal Procedure
laws.excerpt: A judge may order non-suspect third parties to provide decryption assistance. Suspects protected by self-incrimination principle.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: System admins compelled; suspects exempt under Coercive Measures Act.

laws.name: Coercive Measures Act (2011)
laws.excerpt: System owners and administrators must surrender necessary passwords. Suspects themselves are exempt.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: Strong nemo tenetur; no compulsion for suspects; regulatory readability obligations only in non-criminal contexts.

laws.name: Strafprozessordnung (StPO)
laws.excerpt: Suspects cannot be compelled to hand over any kind of cryptographic key due to the nemo tenetur principle.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: Charter s.11(c) protects against compelled self-incrimination. No statutory key-disclosure law. Strongest Five Eyes protections.

laws.name: Charter of Rights and Freedoms (1982)
laws.excerpt: No legislative power can require individuals to decrypt encrypted communications. The federal government has recognised it has no legislative authority to compel individuals to provide a password.

jurisdictionRisk.summary: NSL Art.43 allows police to search/seize electronic devices and compel assistance without judicial oversight for national security matters; Schedule 6 para 3 imposes statutory non-disclosure obligation on assisting parties. Pre-NSL, ICSO Cap.589 required panel judge authorization; post-2020 NSL creates a parallel track with executive authorization and no independent oversight.

laws.name: Interception of Communications and Surveillance Ordinance (Cap. 589)
laws.section: ICSO — superseded by NSL for national security matters

jurisdictionRisk.summary: Art.126m(6) DCCP compels third parties with knowledge of an encryption method to assist decryption when a serious offence is suspected; cannot target the suspect (Art.126m(7)). Judicial oversight via public prosecutor order. No compelled issuance mechanism or statutory gag.

laws.name: Code of Criminal Procedure (Wetboek van Strafvordering)

jurisdictionRisk.summary: LECrim Art.588ter (Organic Law 13/2015) requires judicial order for interception of telecommunications. LGTel Art.39.11 requires operators to deliver communications free of encryption effects where reversible. Judicial oversight required throughout; no statutory compelled issuance or gag.

Law 9.296/1996 Art.1 requires judicial order for interception; providers must make available technological resources to suspend confidentiality including decryption where provider has capability. Brazilian courts have applied this aggressively — executives arrested and services suspended to compel compliance (WhatsApp, 2015–2016). No compelled issuance statute; no gag provision.

Presidential Decree 47 compels service providers to decrypt communications and stored data on competent authority request. Law 2225/1994 as amended governs lawful interception; judicial order required. No purpose-built key seizure statute targeting CA signing keys; no compelled issuance mechanism; no statutory gag.

BÜPF (SR 780.1) Art.22 requires providers to hand over available data under judicial order. No general key-disclosure mandate in current law; proposed VÜPF Art.50a decryption requirement is not yet enacted (consultation closed May 2025, outcome pending). No compelled issuance mechanism; no gag provision.

distrustEvents.summary: Google documented years of misissuance incidents including test certificates, non-audited intermediates, and BR violations. DigiCert acquired Symantec's CA business and managed the transition. Gradual distrust over 12+ months with subscriber migration.
distrustEvents.postureEvidence: Third-party RA program was knowingly structured to bypass validation controls. Repeatedly minimized severity and argued rules should not apply as written. Willful misissuance in training infrastructure. Pattern of argumentative engagement with root programs eroded confidence.

distrustEvents.summary: TurkTrust was distrusted following a pattern of compliance failures including issuing non-audited, non-constrained intermediate certificates and failing to respond to root program surveys. The distrust was triggered by the 2012 incident where their operational mistake led to a fraudulent Google certificate, followed by ongoing compliance deficiencies.

articles.title: Turkish CA enabled phishers to spoof Google
Enhancing digital certificate security

distrustEvents.summary: Certinomis was distrusted in 2019 following a sustained pattern of 20 documented incidents over 2+ years showing systematic BR violations including invalid DNS names, improper certificate profiles, and OCSP failures. Despite being aware of these issues through bug reports, the CA failed to implement effective systemic remediation, with the same violation categories recurring throughout the period.

articles.title: Mozilla distrusts Certinomis issued certificates

distrustEvents.summary: PROCERT was a Venezuelan CA that demonstrated incompetence through non-BR-compliant issuance and complete non-responsiveness to Mozilla's action items. The sparse 2017 bug trail with no CA engagement suggests an organization that lacked the operational capacity to participate meaningfully in the WebPKI ecosystem.

articles.title: Mozilla distrusts PROCERT: local CAs have global impact

distrustEvents.summary: Camerfirma was distrusted after years of systematic Baseline Requirements violations, delayed revocations, and unauthorized subordinate CA issuance. Despite repeated incidents and Mozilla oversight, the CA failed to implement effective controls, with the same types of violations recurring over multiple years.

articles.title: Chrome and Mozilla distrust Camerfirma certificates

distrustEvents.summary: TrustCor was distrusted in 2022 primarily due to discovered corporate ties to surveillance entities rather than the technical compliance issues shown in these 2019 Bugzilla reports. While they had routine compliance problems and delayed revocations, the fundamental issue was organizational trust incompatibility.

articles.title: Mozilla and Microsoft distrust TrustCor root certificates
TrustCor linked to intelligence operations

distrustEvents.summary: Visa demonstrated a pattern of BR violations and audit deficiencies from 2017-2020 while completely failing to engage with root programs or respond to identified issues. The CA showed no meaningful participation in the WebPKI ecosystem it was supposed to serve.

articles.title: Visa Certificate Authority in trouble

distrustEvents.summary: E-Tugra was distrusted after security researcher Ian Carroll discovered severe operational security failures including default passwords and exposed administrative interfaces. The CA had a 4-year pattern of baseline requirements violations but the security research findings triggered immediate distrust action.

articles.title: Security research findings on e-Tugra

distrustEvents.summary: Ecommerce Monitoring demonstrated fundamental operational incompetence through a sustained pattern of baseline requirements violations and delayed revocations spanning 2021-2024. Most notably, when asked for root cause analysis of incidents, they confused the investigative concept with their root certificate, revealing they didn't understand basic CA operational requirements.

distrustEvents.summary: Entrust demonstrated a multi-year pattern of baseline requirements violations, delayed revocations, and argumentative responses that prioritized justifying non-compliance over fixing issues. Chrome explicitly noted Entrust's pattern of arguing that established practices should not apply to their circumstances rather than taking responsibility for mistakes.

tabIntros.note: Analyst summaries generated by Claude from the prior day's snapshot. Each paragraph states the key finding for that tab with specific numbers and connects to related tabs.

intros.market: Five CAs control 92% of all publicly trusted certificate issuance, led by Internet Security Research Group at 40% and Google Trust Services at 19%. The ecosystem includes 89 trusted CAs, but 75 operate in the long tail with minimal market presence. Market concentration has intensified to an HHI of 2346, well above the 1800 threshold economists use to flag competitive concerns, while the top three CAs alone command 72% of issuance.
intros.trust: The four major browser trust stores collectively hold 335 root certificates, but only 90 roots appear in all four stores and just 38 CA owners achieve universal inclusion. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating significant store disagreement that complicates certificate chain validation across browsers. This fragmentation means a certificate chain trusted in Edge may fail in Chrome or Safari, forcing CAs to maintain multiple issuance paths and introducing operational complexity for both CAs and relying parties.
intros.conc: The CR3 concentration of 72% and HHI of 2346 indicate the WebPKI operates as a tight oligopoly where three organizations control nearly three-quarters of all issuance. This systemic dependency creates single points of failure where operational issues or distrust events at Internet Security Research Group or Google Trust Services would immediately affect the majority of HTTPS connections worldwide. The gap between the five dominant CAs and the 75 in the long tail has widened into a two-tier system where market power concentrates while operational scrutiny spreads thin.
intros.tail: Seventy-five CAs operate with minimal issuance volume yet hold full inclusion in one or more browser trust stores, creating asymmetric risk where each carries the technical capability to issue for any domain but lacks the operational scale that attracts sustained oversight. These tail CAs represent the majority of the 89 trusted entities but contribute only 8% of issuance, meaning incident rates and governance attention remain diluted across organizations that rarely face public scrutiny. The long tail persists because browser trust store removal requires affirmative action, while inclusion remains sticky even as issuance approaches zero.
intros.geo: United States-based CAs issue 90% of all publicly trusted certificates despite representing only 15 of 89 trusted CAs, while 44 European CAs collectively account for 10% and 17 Asia-Pacific CAs manage less than 0.1%. This geographic concentration means American corporate governance, labor law, and civil litigation norms effectively set operational standards for the global WebPKI. The issuance disparity vastly exceeds the entity count disparity, indicating European and Asian CAs occupy the long tail while US-headquartered organizations dominate the market share leaders.
intros.gov: Thirty state-operated or state-owned CAs hold trusted roots across the four browser stores but collectively issue only 0.05% of certificates, placing them firmly in the long tail with minimal public web presence. Their inclusion creates potential jurisdiction risk exposure disproportionate to their issuance volume, as government-controlled CAs answer to national interests rather than commercial incentives. This trust surface exists largely as legacy inclusion, maintained through inertia rather than active operational necessity for public HTTPS.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions pose high legal risk due to frameworks enabling compelled access or surveillance without meaningful judicial oversight: China, Russia, United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey present moderate risk with legal authorities that could compel CA access under certain conditions but with more constrained scope. These jurisdiction risks intersect with geographic concentration, as UK-based CAs operate under the Investigatory Powers Act while US-headquartered CAs issuing 90% of certificates face FISA authorities and national security letter frameworks.
intros.ops: CAs have disclosed 1,511 incidents across 54 organizations, with misissuance leading at 588 events followed by governance failures at 476 and revocation issues at 325. Self-detection accounts for only 24% of discoveries while external researchers find 19%, automated tools 17%, and root programs just 4%, revealing a systemic gap where CAs fail to identify their own compliance breakdowns. Policy failures appear in 174 incidents and disclosure failures in 129, indicating the operational breakdowns extend beyond technical misissuance into process adherence and transparency.
intros.crypto: Root certificate algorithms and key sizes across the 335 trusted roots show the ecosystem remains in transition from SHA-1 and 2048-bit RSA to SHA-256 and stronger keys, with legacy roots persisting in trust stores long after their cryptographic relevance expired. Modern issuance concentrates on standards-compliant configurations, but the trust surface still includes roots that predate current baseline requirements and carry weaker cryptographic parameters. This creates a gap between what CAs currently issue and what browsers still trust, with store cleanup lagging behind operational reality.
intros.distrust: Sixteen distrust events across the CA ecosystem break down into negligent noncompliance (7 cases), demonstrated incompetence (3), and willful circumvention (3), with browsers granting a median runway of 1,185 days before full removal. Ten distrust events followed a pattern of repeated issues rather than isolated incidents, and 14 involved compliance operations failures rather than novel technical attacks. The distrust posture distribution shows most cases stem from operational neglect rather than malice, yet browsers have consistently chosen long glide paths that leave problematic CAs trusted for years after initial findings.
intros.policy: The WebPKI regulatory surface has grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6,664 total obligations, with 76% classified as mandatory requirements spanning CA/B Forum baseline requirements, four root program policies, WebTrust and ETSI audit criteria, and supporting standards. Of 40 active TLS CAs measured, only 11 demonstrate readiness for the 47-day maximum validity arriving in March 2029, while 4 remain at risk even for the 200-day limit already in effect and 6 face exposure at the 100-day threshold coming in March 2027. The median CA currently operates at 63-day certificate lifespans, but the compliance burden of navigating thousands of evolving obligations makes operational adaptation slower than ballot timelines assume, particularly as zero ballots have passed since 2022 to rationalize or consolidate requirements.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has collapsed from 68% (Chrome) and 78% (Mozilla) of incidents in 2019 to just 18% and 10% respectively in 2025, with Apple at 5% and Microsoft at 0% across 223 total incidents. Mozilla has generated substantive comments in 816 oversight bugs while Chrome reached 721, but recent substantive engagement shows Chrome at 109 bugs versus Mozilla's 47, indicating shifting attention patterns as overall coverage declines. Microsoft's complete absence from public incident oversight leaves a quarter of root store decisions without visible policy enforcement, creating a governance gap where 142 Microsoft-only roots face no documented scrutiny.
intros.community: The CA/Browser Forum includes 56 members but only 21 contribute actively to ballot or policy work, leaving 35 with zero participation despite holding voting rights and trust store inclusion. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo leads individual ballot activity with 36 proposals, while Sectigo as an organization shows the highest organizational engagement, revealing concentration in standards development that mirrors market concentration. This silent majority pattern means a small fraction of trusted CAs shape the requirements all 89 must follow, with most tail CAs consuming policy rather than contributing to its formation.
intros.audit: Auditors operating under WebTrust and ETSI frameworks caught only 31% of incidents within the audit period when comparing audit letter findings to actual Bugzilla incident histories, revealing a systemic surveillance gap where 69% of operational failures go undetected in assurance letters. Thirty-seven CAs show high transparency gaps between audit dates and public letter availability, 5 received qualified opinions, and 13 changed auditors in 2025 alone, suggesting audit shopping or relationship instability. Self-reported findings account for 59% of WebTrust letters and 66% of ETSI reports, meaning CAs control most of what enters the audit record while the 1,511 incidents logged in Bugzilla demonstrate auditors systematically miss the operational breakdowns that root programs ultimately discover.
